title_patterns: [AI SECTOR] entry timing — which measurable conditions would justify buying?
[NUMBER] [SECTOR] companies — compare valuation with business growth
[NAMED ANALYST]'s [COMPANY OR SECTOR] thesis — assumptions, evidence and countercase
[COMPANY] revenue scenario — what would need to happen to support [VALUATION]?
[COMPANY] insider purchases: [DOLLAR AMOUNT] over [TIME WINDOW] — how material is that?
[COMPANY] after [EARNINGS OR PRICE MOVE] — what changed in the numbers?
hook_patterns: Hypothesis: Open with one verified event or figure, then ask which valuation assumption it changes.
Hypothesis: Present two competing explanations for a company-specific move, then name the metric that could distinguish them.
Hypothesis: Translate a headline dollar amount into a relevant denominator before discussing its significance.
Hypothesis: Use a brief original analogy: 'A lower price is the sale sticker; valuation is the receipt.' Then introduce the comparison.
packaging_notes: AI entry timing has recent strong-tier support: the October 4 candidate has 78,047 views and an 8.9x baseline ratio. Earlier strong-tier AI examples support numbered comparisons and expert framing, but are not all from this week.

Keep tiers separate: the October 10 NVIDIA target-level video is emerging at 2.9x, while the October 4 JPMorgan strategist video is emerging at 5.1x because its channel exceeds the strong-tier subscriber limit. Neither establishes a strong-tier weekly pattern.

Observed strong-tier runtimes span 54 seconds to 31:29; AI timing examples run 54–60 seconds, while expert-led examples span 5:41–31:29. These are format references, not proven duration sweet spots; the <=180-second bucket does not establish Shorts status.

Counts, dollar amounts, time windows and explicit scenarios offer concrete framing. Financial numbers in source titles are unverified claims, not established facts; verify them before reuse and preserve distinctions such as bull case versus base case.

Reject crash, explosion, accusation and urgent-buy language; retain the underlying company-specific question. View-to-baseline ratios are not equal-age comparisons, and metadata cannot establish title causality, retention, effective opening lines or comedy use.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns: For Shorts, a compact company-or-ticker → price move → named catalyst structure appears among several strong retainers. Explicit move percentages accompany 82.8–97.3% average viewing, but this small sample does not establish an optimal number size.

For insider Shorts, company → executive role → buy/sell action → dollar amount is a promising compact structure: two examples retain 93.3–94.0% on average. Lead with the transaction rather than filing mechanics; actual opening scripts were not supplied.
losing_patterns: The two long videos use transaction headlines extended with filing-process detail. Their average viewing is 38.1–46.5%, with hook-window retention of 0.633–0.678. Treat paperwork-heavy framing as a tentative concern, not a proven cause; duration and format are confounded.

Do not rely on a dramatic action verb or large transaction amount to carry a Short. The weakest Shorts average 66.3–69.0% viewing despite those elements; neither excitement nor numerical scale consistently predicts retention.
notes: The sample contains 10 Shorts and only two long videos, with 45–826 views each. Shorts and long-video results should remain separate; these are correlations, not evidence that title structure increases distribution.

Market-close Shorts include several strong retainers, while insider Shorts span 69.0–156.1% average viewing. Neither franchise is uniformly stronger. The 156.1% result on 92 views is replay-compatible, not proof of broad demand.

Average viewing is not swipe-away or feed conversion. Hook-window values above 1 should not be interpreted as unique-viewer survival rates; titles and aggregate retention alone cannot identify which spoken hook framing worked.
